original_incident_edges.relationship: Women and marriage à la façon du pays at the centre of fur-trade society, and missionary racism against Native wives in Red River (1980–86)
original_incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period. 'Many Tender Ties' (1980) is unread here and is quoted only as Bowsfield quotes it (Archivaria 12, 1981, review article, read in full; he gives no page references to the book). He reports her purpose as showing that the fur trade 'constituted a social and cultural complex as well as an economic activity'. He quotes her claims that 'If a man formed a liaison with a woman she was considered to be his wife, entitled to the recognition and support that a marital relationship implied' and that Indian women's work 'constituted an important contribution to the functioning of the trade'. He paraphrases her account of a marriage rite à la façon du pays and of the later turn from Indian to mixed-descent and then white wives, as younger officers became 'imbued with the Victorian middle-class desire for respectability and success' (p. 124). Gagan and Turner (Archivaria 14, 1982, read in full) summarise her argument that these marriages, 'generations of scandalized references notwithstanding, were crucial to the establishment of early western society' (p. 43). Her own words, 1986 (Manitoba History 11, web edition, read in full; no page numbers): 'Fur trade society in Rupert's Land had resulted from decades of inter-marriage among incoming white fur traders with Indian and later mixed-blood women'; 'Racist attitudes, particularly with regard to women, can be seen in the attempts of the missionaries to enforce their concepts of morality upon a society that had developed its own indigenous customs.' Brown (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, read in full) takes 'the work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) on the socioeconomic role of women in the fur trade' as one starting point for Métis history (p. 40). Criticism: Bowsfield notes her view that such unions were not 'casual' or 'promiscuous' and comments, 'This may be too complimentary a picture of both native women and European men' (p. 124). LaRocque's criticism (1999) is recorded on pe139_vankirk_rel_04, and edge_868 carries the Indigenous critiques at entry level. Not a founding: Bowsfield reviews the book within a fur-trade literature already recast by Ray, Trigger and others (pp. 121–24). Later reading, labelled: Perry (Left History 13:2, 2008, read in full) writes that 'In the early 1990s Van Kirk's work particularly garnered some sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques, ones that made clear how wedded "Many Tender Ties" was to a Eurocentric, celebratory sort of liberal feminism', and then that Van Kirk's and Brown's 'symbiotic arguments about the centrality of women and family to the Canadian fur-trade' have 'never been cast into serious doubt' (p. 163). The critiques she cites (n. 7: Pierson 1992; Emberley 1990–91) are unread here.

original_incident_edges.relationship: Indigenous and mixed-descent women written into Canadian women's history, with race as a division among women (1980–98)
original_incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period. As Bowsfield quotes the book (Archivaria 12, 1981, p. 124; no page given), Van Kirk claimed that it 'supports the claims of theorists in women's history that sex roles should constitute a category of historical investigation', and she admitted the limits of relying on male sources. He finds 'a feminist note to some of Van Kirk's statements but it must be admitted that it is not a strident one'. Gagan and Turner's survey of Canadian social history (Archivaria 14, 1982, p. 29 and n. 7) puts 'Many Tender Ties' and Strangers in Blood under women's work: 'two noteworthy recent studies attempt to recreate the whole way of life of a particular group of "working" women, those who participated in the Canadian fur trade', in which 'the whole woman-wife, mother, labourer, diplomat, chattel, entrepreneur-is revealed'. Her own words, 1986 (Manitoba History 11, read in full): 'Other important themes for women's history also emerge'; 'The reasons for such "unsisterly" action should be confronted squarely by feminist historians'; 'The rivalry among women in nineteenth century Red River, however, was compounded by the issue of race'; and 'The racism evinced by white women in Red River, while as inexcusable as that of their male counterparts, was aggravated by what, in their view, was a concrete threat to their own welfare in the competition for eligible husbands.' 1997–98 (BC Studies 115/116, pp. 149–51 read): 'Little attention has been paid to the fact that this process of acculturation was gendered'; 'a complex interaction of gender and class dynamics, coupled with the particular demographics of early Victoria, enabled the girls to transcend the racist climate of the colony more successfully than the boys' (p. 150). Reception in a Canadian women's studies journal, 2000 (Atlantis 25:1, both read in full): McPherson calls the book a 'now-classic work' and writes that 'Van Kirk's research and the critical debates it has aroused have played a crucial role in writing Native women into western Canadian history and in bringing cultural difference and conflict into Canadian women's history' (p. 82). Fiske writes that understanding the discursive formation of Aboriginal women's sexuality 'requires us to build on the early work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) and Jennifer Brown (1980) by placing Aboriginal women in the context of the expectations held of settler women' (p. 12); this extends the work rather than rejecting it. Pierson's 'Colonization and Canadian Women's History' (1992) cites the book (OpenAlex reference list only; text unread). Criticism is recorded on rel_01 (Bowsfield) and rel_04 (LaRocque). edge_872 compares the two field entries at title level; this edge adds her own words and the field's reading of her.

original_incident_edges.relationship: Two 1980 studies of fur-trade marriage and family, read as a pair: women and marriage (Van Kirk) and company officers' families and descent (Brown)
original_incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period. Bowsfield (Archivaria 12, 1981, read in full) reviews the books together: 'In Strangers in Blood Jennifer Brown, using basically the same sources and employing the same macrobiographical approach as Van Kirk, examines the fur traders group looking at their social background, their domestic lives, their family relationships, and the fate of their children'. He singles out Brown's 'comparison between Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company men as husbands and fathers' (p. 124). He concludes: 'With Van Kirk and Brown the unique and complex role of women and the fur trade family unit have been opened to investigation', and 'Through the study of fur trade families a distinctive Canadian approach to family history has been developed' (p. 126). Gagan and Turner (1982, p. 29, n. 7) cite the two books in one note as studies of working women. Brown (CJNS, 1983, read in full) builds on both books. 'Another starting point for this discussion is the work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) on the socioeconomic role of women in the fur trade' (p. 40); 'A third incentive for writing this paper comes from pursuing the implications of what I have called the patrifocality that characterized some upper-level fur trade families' (p. 41). Their own in-period words differ in frame. Van Kirk writes of 'themes for women's history' and of what 'feminist historians' should confront, among women divided by race in Red River (1986). Brown uses the anthropological models of 'matriorganization' and 'unilocality' to ask how women and descent shaped 'metis emergence' (1983, pp. 40–42). LaRocque (1999, PDF p. 249) criticises both in one list. Later readings, labelled. Brown (2012, read in the 2017 reprint) recalls: 'We became, it seemed, the Bobbsey Twins of fur trade social history, often cited in the same breath or footnote by writers who might or might not have read our books' (p. 187). She also says that 'her sphere of work and teaching increasingly became women's history, while mine focused more on Aboriginal history' (p. 191), and that Van Kirk 'tended to accept more as given' categories such as 'marriage,' 'custom,' and 'society' (pp. 191–92). Van Kirk 'had a devotion to the ones that worked', whereas 'my book title, Strangers in Blood, picked up on a different angle' (p. 192). Brown quotes Van Kirk's letter of 1972: 'As an anthropologist you will likely be applying a different set of criteria to the primary source material' (p. 184); the letter is known here only through that 2012 quotation. Perry (2008) writes that 'Brown's analysis placed family and kinship at the centre of fur-trade life, and Van Kirk's argued for the centrality of women' (p. 162), and calls their arguments 'symbiotic' (p. 163). This is a comparison, and no direction is asserted. Each person's contribution sits on her own edges to native_newcomer.

original_incident_edges.relationship: LaRocque: cross-cultural ethnological description of Native and Métis women as othering, 1999
original_incident_edges.evidence_note: Emma LaRocque's specified criticism in her 1999 University of Manitoba dissertation (read at PDF pp. 54 and 249); the arrow leaves from her entry since revision 1.204 (it left from the Indigenous history entry before her entry existed). She describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)', which 'tended to frame all things Native in typical terms of "cultural differences" or "traditions."' She grants: 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history. And with greater awareness, there is greater improvement.' But 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect', and 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience' (p. 249). Her note 18 names the book: 'See in Many Tender Ties, for example, Van Kirk's listing of all the items of fashion or jewelry metis women were "very fond of" (101-103). There is an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable" for these women to acquire' (p. 249, n. 18). In an earlier note she cites the book, with Saum and Ray and Freeman, among fur-trade studies that record Native resistance (PDF p. 54, note). Brown is named in the same list on p. 249 and the criticism is noted on her own entry (pe139_brown_rel_01); one arrow is drawn, to Van Kirk, because the note's example is hers. edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer) already carries LaRocque with Sioui and Stevenson (Wheeler) at entry level; this edge records the person-level target. OCR slips in the PDF text layer are corrected ('Van Krk', 'al1', 'hrterests'). The page numbers are PDF pages, as in edge_868. No identity classification is recorded. Later reading, labelled: Perry (2008, p. 163) dates 'sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques' of Van Kirk's work to the early 1990s; those texts are unread here.

original_incident_edges.relationship: Mixed-race relationships not to be explained by white women's absence: Perry's 1995 criticism of fur-trade historians, Van Kirk's 'brilliant account' included, for treating intermarriage as the product of that absence, and her 2001 argument (as Carter reports it) that such relationships were 'not confined to the fur trade' and that 'happy stories' of fur-trade marriages can 'obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism'
original_incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 1995 (BC Studies 105/106, read at p. 30): 'Historians of the fur trade, while concerned with establishing the salience of mixed-race relationships, nonetheless explain their frequency as the product of white women's absence'; n. 8: 'For a brilliant account which ultimately suggests that the existence of mixed-race relationships was the result of white women's absence from the fur trade, see Sylvia Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" … Also see Jennifer S. H. Brown, Strangers in Blood … and Robin Fisher, Contact and Conflict'; n. 11 quotes Van Kirk: 'Had it been possible for fur traders to bring their wives out at an earlier date, it is doubtful whether intermarriage with native women would have been so extensive' (Many Tender Ties, p. 173); the 'volcano theory' 'holds that mixed-race relationships are at worst unfathomable and at best the products of abnormal historical circumstances' (p. 30). Qualifications kept: the criticism is of one explanation, not of the field; she calls Van Kirk's account 'brilliant' (p. 30 n. 8) and 'pioneering' (p. 43), and relies on it for the displacement of Aboriginal women (p. 43). 2001: the book is unread; Carter (BC Studies 136, p. 118, read) reports that 'Perry does not write a history of these relationships, noting the difficulties with available sources, but she does argue that they were not confined to the fur trade and could be found in the city, in the country, and in mining towns', and that she 'stresses the need to look beyond the "happy stories," such as the long marriage of James Douglas and Amelia Connolly, that can "obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism" (62)'. In-period counterpoint: Orlowski (2002, p. 121, read) faults the book because 'the mixed-race couples in colonial B.C. had much to do with building alliances, sometimes between Hudson's Bay Company officers and the daughters of Aboriginal chiefs, a strategy that is not considered at all in the book'. No reply by Van Kirk or Brown was checked. Later reading, labelled: in 2016 (p. 113) she proposes thinking 'seriously about fur-trade colonialism as a distinct and meaningful practice of empire' (Colonial Relations, on the Douglas–Connolly family, is unread). Target: Van Kirk's person entry, since the criticism is of her explanation of intermarriage; her entry cites Perry's 2008 essay on her work only as a later reading.

live_incident_edges.relationship: Brown explicitly uses Van Kirk’s account of Indigenous women’s productive work in the fur trade as a starting point for asking how women shaped emerging Métis families and communities.
live_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 1983:40–41 names Many Tender Ties (1980) and uses fur preparation, snowshoe production, foraging and intergenerational transmission to generate questions about women’s economic roles and continuity. Source explicitly says records may fail to confirm some propositions; not universal proof or sole origin of her research. Bishop/Krech, Asch and Peterson remain distinct resources. This directed particular resource is different from existing 1002 paired-book comparison. Original 1980 book unread; fresh 1983 article checked.

live_incident_edges.relationship: Brown qualifies Van Kirk’s treatment of marriage, custom and society as comparatively given categories, while praising her archival attentiveness and warning that modern theory can also obscure historical voices.
live_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own essay written for 2012 volume, checked in 2017 recast 191–192, contrasts her anthropological category questioning with Van Kirk’s historical training. She immediately credits Van Kirk’s strengths, and 192 admits both shared bias toward unions that worked. This is limited conceptual qualification, not wholesale charge of romanticism or theoretical incompetence. Existing 1002 comparison preserved different kind; underlying 1980 books and original 2012 printing unread. Geertz/Bhabha 191 are hypothetical outside-theory examples, not unambiguous targets of direct reading.

live_incident_edges.relationship: Carter uses Van Kirk’s analysis of changing interracial marriage to explain hostility toward Indigenous women’s marriages within the later settler order.
live_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2008: 6 explicitly attributes the changing hostility to Van Kirk. Chapter 1 note 12 identifies the 2006 reprint of From Marrying-In to Marrying-Out in the Gleason/Perry edited Rethinking Canada, with Van Kirk’s 1980 Many Tender Ties and Perry’s 2001 book as further resources. This is a specified historical resource within Carter’s argument, not direct mentoring, sole credit for every fur-trade marriage claim, or independent verification of those originals. Existing group comparisons are not a Van Kirk→Carter personal claim.

Greer’s claims about aggregate subsistence output remain his unreplicated argument.
